newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico central bank charts new money market course.
newsitem.headline: Mexico central bank charts new money market course.

text.p: Economists are wondering how long a new phase in Mexico's monetary policy will continue, one that has seen Banco de Mexico drain liquidity from money markets since the start of the year.
The sea change in the central bank's money market objective may even be expanded, some economists said on Tuesday.
On January 9, Banco de Mexico began draining liquidity through deposit auctions in money markets instead of its usual practice of providing credits.

The central bank has sought to unwind some of the large seasonal increase in cash that pushed up the monetary base late last year. "This process will probably continue until the end of the month. It is a natural process," said Vector Casa de Bolsa economist Rodolfo Navarrete.
But other economists say the central bank may have an even broader motive, aiming to offset large amounts of foreign capital flowing into Mexico as the country's economy improves.
The central bank has also been providing commercial banks with pesos through its peso put option mechanism, which allows it to also build dollar reserves.
Moreover, funds are making their way into the system via Pemex, as the central bank buys dollars from the state-owned oil company and converts them into pesos, analysts said.
But that increased peso liquidity must be soaked up or sterilized to prevent an unwanted increase in the monetary base, they add.
So in order to prevent excessive liquidity from putting downward pressure on interest rates, the central bank reversed its daily credit auctions, brokerage Valores Finamex said in a report.

"Instead of pumping out liquidity, it has begun drawing it in, or, in other words, sterilizing dollar flows," Valores Finamex economist Ann Ginsburg said. "With the likely continued success of the options program and expected stability in oil prices, the deposit auction is likely to be used for some time."
She added that some variations may be introduced, such as the exchange of collateral by the central bank for the deposits to help lower its "borrowing costs."

"A series of announcements, such as the prepayment of debt (to the U.S. Treasury) and the (global) bond placement, have unleashed a better flow of funds towards the country, which means the authorities have had to counteract the excess of liquidity in the system," said one Mexico City-based money market analyst who declined to be identified.
He said that as key mid-term Congressional and state elections set for July 6 approach, market volatility and nervousness could cause the central bank to start to offer credits again.
Commercial banks built up large amounts of debt with the central bank in 1994 and that has been constantly refinanced with new credits through the daily credit auctions.
Banco de Mexico has gradually reduced this burden of outstanding debt though periodic Cetes buybacks, which it could choose to do again, Valores Finamex's Ginsburg said.

She added that the targeted cumulative balance will continue to be used the manage interest rates. A preference for higher interest rates would be achieved by auctioning more deposits, since the central bank is now competing with other borrowers in the interbank system.
She said that if liquidity moved to a short supply, the central bank could resume the credit auctions.
"But in the meantime, Banxico will continue to run deposit auctions, ending the two-year phase of daily credit auctions made necessary by the banking system liquidity crunch of 1994," Ginsburg said.
